identity.title: Cheating Automatic LLM Benchmarks: Null Models Achieve High Win Rates

problem.claim: Assess whether automatic LLM benchmarks can be gamed despite mechanisms intended to control output length and style.

gap.claim: The abstract reports that existing controls do not prevent a constant, input-irrelevant null model from attaining top-ranked benchmark results.

contributions.claim: Demonstrates that a constant-response null model can achieve high scores across three automatic LLM benchmarks.
Reports transferable cheating outputs under the assumption that benchmark instructions and samples are private.
Calls for anti-cheating mechanisms to improve automatic benchmark reliability.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their demonstration by showing that an always-constant, input-irrelevant null model can reach top-ranked win rates on multiple benchmarks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report an 86.5% LC win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0, an 83.0 score on Arena-Hard-Auto, and a 9.55 score on MT-Bench for the null model.
The authors report that crafted cheating outputs transfer when benchmark instructions are assumed private, including 805 AlpacaEval 2.0 samples.
The authors characterize the experiments as primarily proof-of-concept and warn that LLM-generated cheating responses could be more imperceptible.

narrative_sequence.summary: Automatic benchmarks are presented as scalable, cost-effective alternatives to human evaluation, while high win rates provide promotional benefits.
The abstract notes that output-length and style manipulation may game win rates despite existing controls.
A constant, irrelevant null response is reported to achieve high or top-ranked results on three benchmarks.
The reported transferability under private-instruction assumptions motivates anti-cheating mechanisms, with ethical risks noted.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a concrete adversarial baseline—a constant response—with benchmark-specific scores across three evaluation systems.

lessons.interpretation: A deliberately degenerate baseline can expose whether an evaluation metric rewards superficial response properties rather than task relevance.
lessons.application: When introducing or auditing a benchmark, add fixed, input-irrelevant response baselines and report their metric scores alongside model results.
lessons.exception: This diagnostic is unsuitable when the benchmark is explicitly designed only for a narrow capability that such a baseline cannot meaningfully target.

source_observation.claim: The authors discuss transferability while assuming benchmark instructions and samples are private.

lessons.interpretation: Robustness claims should account for attackers who lack direct access to evaluation prompts.
lessons.application: Evaluate cheating defenses under both public-prompt and private-prompt threat models, stating the access assumptions explicitly.
lessons.exception: A private-prompt threat model is unsuitable when the deployed evaluation protocol necessarily exposes all prompts.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide benchmark baselines, statistical uncertainty, ranking thresholds, or experimental procedures.
The meaning and scale of the reported Arena-Hard-Auto and MT-Bench scores are not specified.
The extent of transferability and the exact construction of cheating outputs are not detailed.
